entries.name: Soybean
entries.spread: East Asia since antiquity; United States and Brazil since the 20th century; now the world's most-grown legume
entries.notes: About three quarters of the crop feeds livestock. Raw soy is inedible to monogastrics (trypsin inhibitors), so all soy food is cooked or fermented.

entries.name: Common bean
entries.spread: The Americas first; spread worldwide after 1500 to every warm continent
entries.notes: One name for kidney, pinto, black, navy and haricot types. The standard dried bean of the Americas and the most eaten pulse by volume after soy.

entries.name: Field pea
entries.wild_ancestor: wild field pea (Pisum sativum subsp. elatius)
entries.spread: Europe, North Africa and India by 3000 BCE; now grown across temperate farmland
entries.notes: One of the eight founder crops of agriculture. Both a dry pulse and a fodder crop; the garden pea is the same species picked young.

entries.name: Groundnut
entries.spread: Tropical and subtropical belts worldwide; a West African staple and the peanut of North American cuisine
entries.notes: Geocarpy: the flower stalk (peg) drives the pod underground after pollination, so it needs loose soil to fruit. In-shell yield; about 45-50% oil.

entries.name: Chickpea
entries.spread: Mediterranean and India since antiquity; India grows the majority of the world crop today
entries.notes: Two trade types: small dark desi and large pale kabuli. Staple for falafel, hummus and chana masala; tolerates poor, near-neutral soil.

entries.name: Lentil
entries.spread: Europe, North Africa and Southwest Asia by 6000 BCE; India and Canada are the modern leaders
entries.notes: Among the very first crops domesticated. Small seed, quick to cook; the base of dals, soups and stews across three continents.

entries.name: Faba bean
entries.spread: Mediterranean, Ethiopia, China and northern Europe; the main Old World cool-season broad bean
entries.notes: Large-seeded and frost-hardy; the ful mudammas of Egypt and the broad bean of British gardens are the same crop.

entries.name: Alfalfa

domesticated.where: Central Asia and the Iranian plateau

entries.spread: Persia to Greece around 490 BCE with the Persian wars; worldwide forage since the Middle Ages
entries.notes: The queen of forages; perennial stands cut 3-6 times a year for 4-8 years. Yield is dry-matter hay; bloat risk if grazed lush by cattle.

entries.name: Cowpea
entries.spread: Sahel and savanna West Africa; spread to Asia, the Mediterranean and the Americas after 1500
entries.notes: Black-eyed pea, niebe, Southern pea: the Sahel's protein in a millet intercrop. The yardlong bean is its long-podded subspecies.

entries.name: Mung bean
entries.spread: India since the Harappan period; East and Southeast Asia from ~2000 BCE; grown worldwide today
entries.notes: The dal and bean-sprout pulse; actual yields (0.5-0.7 t/ha) badly trail its 1.8-2.5 t/ha potential, a classic yield-gap study crop.

entries.name: Pigeon pea
entries.spread: South and Southeast Asia, East and southern Africa and the Caribbean; the dal crop of semi-arid India
entries.notes: A shrubby perennial used as a live fallow and hedge as well as a pulse. Short-duration cultivars run 90 days; traditional ones take 200-300.

entries.name: Lima bean
entries.spread: The Americas before Columbus; grown worldwide for butter-like dried beans and green limas
entries.notes: Named for Lima, Peru. Two gene pools: large-seeded Andean and small-seeded Mesoamerican Sieva types. Raw wild seeds are cyanogenic.

entries.name: Adzuki bean
entries.spread: East Asia; the red bean of anko, mochi and festive sweets; now also a health-food pulse in the West
entries.notes: Small brick-red bean, usually boiled soft with sugar. The second-most-important legume of East Asia after soybean.

entries.name: White lupin
entries.spread: Mediterranean since antiquity; modern sweet varieties grown in Europe, Australia and Chile
entries.notes: Ancient bitter fodder crop debittered by soaking; modern sweet cultivars need no soaking. Very high protein for grain or forage.

entries.name: Black gram
entries.wild_ancestor: wild black gram (Vigna mungo var. silvestris)
entries.spread: India and Southeast Asia; the urad dal of South Indian cuisine
entries.notes: Essential to fermented idli and dosa batter. Related to mung but black-seeded; a major kharif pulse in India.

entries.name: Grass pea
entries.spread: Balkans, Mediterranean, Ethiopia and India; a famine-reserve pulse for the dry and the poor
entries.notes: Survives where other crops die, but eats that make it more than ~30% of the diet cause lathyrism (irreversible leg paralysis) from the ODAP toxin. Low-ODAP varieties and processing lower the risk.

entries.name: Fenugreek
entries.spread: Near East to India; seeds in curries and spice blends, leaves as methi greens, sprouts worldwide
entries.notes: Charred seeds found at Tell Halal (Iraq, ~4000 BCE) and in Tutankhamun's tomb. Sprouts triggered the 2011 German E. coli outbreak; treat sprout lots as a hazard.

entries.name: Horsegram
entries.spread: Indian subcontinent and Sri Lanka; a drought refuge pulse of the Deccan plateau
entries.notes: Grows where nothing else will; the traditional famine food of dry India. Yield reflects the marginal land it tolerates, not poor breeding.

entries.name: Lablab bean
entries.spread: India since at least 1500 BCE; Sudan and East Africa; cultivated across the tropics
entries.notes: Hyacinth bean: twining, ornamental purple pods and flowers as well as a hardy dal. Also grown as a green manure and animal forage.

entries.name: Bambara groundnut
entries.wild_ancestor: wild bambara groundnut (Vigna subterranea var. spontanea)
entries.spread: Sub-Saharan Africa; largely displaced by the imported peanut but valued for resilience
entries.notes: Like the peanut it ripens pods underground (geocarpy), but needs far less water and care. Nearly balanced protein; women-grown crop, central to Sahelian food security.

entries.name: Tepary bean

domesticated.where: southwestern North America and northwestern Mexico

entries.spread: Southwest US and Sonora; nearly vanished, now being revived as a climate-change pulse
entries.notes: Needs perhaps a third the water of a common bean. O'odham and Pueblo crop rediscovered as a model for arid agriculture.

entries.name: Scarlet runner bean
entries.spread: Central America; a cottage-garden climber in Europe since the 17th century
entries.notes: Grown for green pods and flowers more than dry seed; spectacular scarlet bloom, beloved by bees. Likes the cool humid UK better than hot dry plains.

entries.name: Rice bean
entries.spread: Mountain Southeast Asia and Southwest China; emerging from obscurity as a hill pulse
entries.notes: Small yellow-brown bean of upland slopes; fast growing, dual-use for grain and sprouts. A candidate pulse for marginal tropical highlands.

entries.name: Moth bean
entries.spread: Rajasthan and Gujarat; one of the driest cultivated legumes anywhere
entries.notes: Prostrate desert pulse needing barely any rain; sprouted and used in sabzi and dal. Hardy even on shifting sand.

entries.name: Red clover
entries.spread: Europe from the 16th century; now the standard short-term clover of temperate grassland
entries.notes: Short-lived perennial, 2-3 year stands, cut for hay or silage. Very high-quality protein forage; needs bumblebees to set seed.

entries.name: Common vetch
entries.spread: Mediterranean since Roman times; standard green-manure and fodder vetch of temperate farms
entries.notes: Dual-purpose: grazed or cut green, or grown as a soil-building green manure before a cereal. Vines scramble if not sown densely.

entries.name: Sainfoin
entries.spread: France and Central Europe; revived for its tannin as a non-bloating forage
entries.notes: 'Holy hay' in French; its tannins prevent bloat, unlike clover and alfalfa. Also an excellent nectar source for pollinators.

entries.name: Bird's-foot trefoil
entries.spread: Eurasia; a low-growing pasture legume of poor and steep ground
entries.notes: Non-bloating trefoil with cyanogenic compounds in trace amounts; persistent in pastures where clover gives up.

entries.name: Velvet bean
entries.spread: India and West Africa since antiquity; the great tropical green-manure cover crop of the modern era
entries.notes: Fixes nitrogen voraciously and smothers weeds; seeds hold L-DOPA, so it is grown for cover, not food. Pod hairs itch fiercely.

entries.name: Jack bean
entries.spread: The Americas; spread by Spain to Asia and Africa as a green manure
entries.notes: Seeds carry canavanine, a toxic non-protein amino acid; strictly a green manure or afterprocessing feed, never eaten plain.

entries.name: Winged bean
entries.spread: New Guinea and equatorial Asia; little known west of it, a cult supercrop on paper
entries.notes: 'One-species supermarket': leaves, flowers, pods, seeds and tubers all edible and protein-rich. Yield here is fresh pods, not dry grain; almost never grown commercially.

entries.name: Tamarind
entries.spread: India since antiquity, now throughout the tropics; the souring agent of countless cuisines
entries.notes: Pulp is the souring backbone of sambar, pad thai and Worcestershire sauce. Yield is pods; long-lived tree, too big for farm plots, best as a landmark block.

entries.name: Carob
entries.spread: Mediterranean since antiquity; orchards in Spain, Italy, Morocco and Portugal
entries.notes: 'St John's bread'; pod pulp sweetens and thickens, seeds supposedly gave us the carat. Yield is pods; slow-bearing tree, full crop only at 20-25 years.

entries.name: African locust bean
entries.spread: West African savanna; the seeds ferment into dawadawa, iru and soumbala condiments
entries.notes: A nitrogen-fixing savanna shade tree whose fermented seeds are the umami of West African cooking. Yield unknown; wild stands are semi-managed, not planted.
